1.1       The Ministry of Small Scale Industries is the nodal ministry for policy formulation, promotion, development and
protection of small scale industries. It also monitors the implementation of these policies.
1.2       Ministry of SSI designs and implements the policies through its field organizations for promotion and growth of
small enterprises. The Ministry also coordinates with other Ministries/Departments on behalf of the Small Scale
Industries (SSI) sector.
1.3       Implementation of   policies and various programmes/schemes for providing infrastructure and support services
to small enterprises is undertaken through its attached office, namely the Small Industries Development Organisation
(SIDO).
1.4              Small Scale Sector is an integral part of the Indian economy. It has contributed significantly in the overall
economic development of the country and has provided vibrancy to its economy. Today, there are 3.2   million
registered small units in the country employing 18 million persons. In terms of value addition, it contributes 40 per cent
of the manufacturing sector production and its share in the total exports of the country is around 36 per cent. This sector
is the largest employment generator next to agriculture.
1.5              The overall performance of this sector during the last few years has been better than the performance of the
industrial sector as a whole. This sector has the potential to withstand change. It produces more than 8,000 items
varying from the simple to the most sophisticated products, using state-of-the-art technology. However, with
liberalization and opening up of the Indian economy, this sector is now facing tremendous challenges, albeit with
sufficient opportunities for growth.
1.6       The process of liberalization and market reforms has created wide-ranging opportunities for the development of
small-scale industries. At the same time, changing world scenario has thrown up new challenges to the very existence of
the sector. Moreover, this sector has also been facing some problems related to credit, infrastructure, technology,
marketing, delayed payments, problems on account of complex rules and regulation etc.  The need of the hour is to
suitably strengthen the sector so that it can adapt itself to the changed environment and face challenges boldly and
effectively. In order to enable this sector to avail the opportunities and play its role as an engine of growth, the Hon’ble
Prime Minister on 30
th August 2000 announced a Comprehensive Policy Package for the SSI Sector.
1.7       The small enterprise has emerged as a focus area for forging and promoting trade. Economic reform programmes
envisage the emergence of Indian Industry as a global competitor with substantial presence in the international markets.
Technology upgradation and modernization of SSI sector and promotion of export from this sector are interlinked
issues, which are important objectives behind promoting international cooperation. Nine countries viz; USA, Germany,
Italy, South Korea, U.K., Taiwan, Japan, Singapore and Israel have been identified as the thrust countries for promoting
enterprise-to-enterprise cooperation to upgrade the capabilities of Indian SSI sector to make it competitive in the global

3.6       The Committee observes that in the context of liberalization and globalisation of the economy, the competitive
strengths of the small scale industries will need to be enhanced through suitable policy measures by which they can be

 3.7      The Committees notes   that measure such as setting up of incubators to assist the growth of small scale industry

Ministry should take steps to provide such measures so as to enable the small entrepreneurs to use the facilities provided
by the incubators as they compete against importers as well as other domestic producers.
3.8       The Committees further observes that it is essential to create greater awareness about the obligations India has to
fulfill under the WTO regime and their impact on various sectors. There is a need to have adequate preparedness for
WTO compliance. The Committee recommends that regular interactions between the Government and SSls should take
place for this purpose.  Special cells with legal backup may be created and strengthened to deal with WTO related
problems of SSls in concerned Government departments and industry associations.

VI.      CREDIT TO SSI SECTOR
6.1       One of the major problems of SSls is that of finance, whether it is equity, term loan or working capital. Financial
institutions and commercial banks are often reluctant to lend to small scale enterprises because of the high risks
involved. Moreover, the commercial banks and financial institutions that provide working capital and term finance to
the corporate borrower generally demand personal guarantees from borrowers, besides collateral. This adversely affects
the borrowing capacity of the small entrepreneur. The lack of coordination between commercial banks and financial
institutions causes delay in availability of working capital and hence in the commissioning of projects. The complex and
time-consuming procedures and formalities of the institutional lenders cause operational impediments for SSI units.
6.2       The Ministry has apprised the Committee that the net bank credit outstanding to SSI sector has increased from
Rs. 45, 789 crores as on 31.3.2000 to Rs. 48, 445 crores on 31.3.2001.  In order to further increase the flow of credit, the

should reschedule holidays of   Public Sector Banks in such a manner that public in general and SSI sector in particular
do not suffer   any more. 
6.6       Encouraged by the Kisan Credit Card Scheme, public sector banks have now decided to introduce a scheme
called Laghu Udyami Credit Card (LUCC) scheme for providing simplified and borrower friendly credit facilities to
small businessmen, retail traders, artisans and, small entrepreneurs, professionals and other self employed persons,
including those in the tiny sector.
6.7       The Committee hopes that this scheme is successful and that the small and tiny sector is able to derive
substantial advantage from it.
 
VII.     CREDIT GUARANTEE FUND SCHEME FOR SMALL INDUSTRIES
7.1       The Government introduced the Credit Guarantee Fund Scheme for Small Industries in May 2000 with the
objective of making credit available to SSI units, particularly tiny units, for loans up to Rs.10 lakh without
collateral/third party guarantees. The Scheme is being operated by the Credit Guarantee Fund Trust for Small Industries
(CGTSI) set up jointly by the Government of India and SIDBI. The loan limit underthe Scheme, which was Rs.10 lakh
per borrower, has been enhanced to Rs.25 lakh per borrower in terms of the Comprehensive Policy Package on SSI
announced by the Hon’ble Prime Minister on 30
th August, 2000, when the Scheme was formally launched.
7.2       The Scheme covers collateral free credit facility (term loan and/or working capital) extended by eligible lending
institutions to new and existing SSI Units including Information Technology and Software Industry, up to Rs.25 lakh
per borrowing unit. The Guarantee cover would be up to 75% of the credit subject to maximum guarantee limit of
Rs.18.75 lakh. The lending institutions availing guarantee from theTrust have to pay a one time guarantee fee of 2.5% of
the Credit facility (comprising term loan and/or working capital) sanctioned by the lending institution to the borrower
and annual service fee of 1% per annum on the outstanding loan amount on 31
st March of each year.
7.3       The Credit Guarantee Scheme was initially approved for one year with a corpus of Rs.125 crore contributed by
the Government of India and SIDBI in the ratio of 4:1. Subsequently, the Government decided to continue the Scheme
beyond one year and increase the eligibility of loans to be guaranteed from Rs.10 lakh to Rs.25 lakh. Necessary
modifications have been carried out in the indenture of the Trust to enable Credit GuaranteeFund Trust for Small
Industries to guarantee loans up to Rs.25 lakh.  The Corpus fund of CGTSI was enhanced to Rs.200 crore with a further

VIII.     VENTURE CAPITAL FUND
8.1       The Committee observes that in order to encourage new entrepreneurs to set up small scale units, it is very
important to create Venture Capital facilities. With a view to meeting the needs of emerging areas and to help the small
scale units in Software / Information Technology sector, SIDBI has taken an initiative in the launching of the State /
Regional Level Venture Capital Fund with participation from State Governments. However, Venture Capital is not
easily available to very small and tiny units. EXIM Bank has also made an entry into venture capital finance by
investing in a Venture Capital Fund -India Technology Venture Unit Scheme -promoted by Unit Trust of India.
8.2       The Committee recommends that more venture funds in high-growth sectors such as information technology,
biotechnology and food processing should be set up. A suitable policy framework may be designed expeditiously to
promote setting up of such funds in the public as well as the private sector. Banks should be encouraged to entertain
Venture Capital funding to SSI units.   India can learn from the Korean experience, which has a very well developed
system of venture capital financing. The Korean Government has also made every effort to provide an atmosphere in
which a new concept company, the venture business, could take root during a short period of time. As a result, the
number of Venture Capital firms has increased tremendously in Korea during the last three to four years.

XI.       ANTI DUMPING MEASURES
11.1     There is expected to be large scale dumping of different products and flow of cheaper imports to Indian markets.
Imported consumer goods being of international standards in quality and competitive in prices are likely to change the
tastes of Indian consumers. It may prove to be a major factor in shrinking demand for local products. SSls are struggling
to restructure themselves, diversify production, adopt higher standards, and have collaborations for product designs or
brands or upgraded technology for their existence. There is ignorance among small scale entrepreneurs about
implications of WTO provisions in general and removal of QRs in particular. SSls did not get much time to adjust and
prepare themselves for increased competition and are thus in a precarious situation.

XII.       SICKNESS IN SSI SECTOR
12.1     The small scale industry in India faces a number of problems leading to growing industrial sickness. According
to the RBI Report on Trend and Progress of Banking in India, there were 3,06,013 sick / weak 551 units in 1999. An
amount of Rs 4,313 crore of outstanding bank credit was locked up in these units. Out of the total sick / weak units,
18,692 units have been identified as potentially viable. Amongst these, 12, 759 have been put under nursing programme
by banks.
12.2     The Ministry has informed that Sickness in SSI Sector is a matter of constant concern. A number of measures
have been taken from time to time to reduce the incidence of sickness in the small scale sector. The incidence of
sickness in the sector has come down consistently from 306,221 sick SSI units as on March 1999 to 2,49,360 sick SSI
units as on March 2001.
  12.3      To tackle the problem of rehabilitation of potentially viable sick SSI units, the RBI constituted a Working
Group on 25th November 2000 under the chairmanship of Shri S.S.Kohli, the then Chairman of Indian Banks
Association, to look into the issue. The Working Group submitted its Report in May 2001. All the major
recommendations of the Working Group have been accepted by the RBI, including a change in the definition of sick SSI
units, norms for deciding on the viability of sick units, etc. The revised definition would enable Banks to take action at
an early stage for revival of the units. Based on the accepted recommendations of the Working Group, the RBI has
drawn up the Revised Guidelines for Rehabilitation of Sick SSI Units, which have been circulated on 16th January 2002
to all the Banks for implementation.
12.4        The Committee recommends that all banks should take effective steps to help sick SSIs restructure
themselves.  The Committee observes that the abolition of Sick Industries Companies Act (SICA) so as to facilitate
prompt winding up of unviable enterprise and swift redeployment of their resources in production remains a promise.
Similarly, on the Competition Law, nothing has been done. It has reached only the stage of Parliamentary consideration.
It has not become a law.

Act.  Further, Ministry should endeavour to see that Competition Law is enacted soon.

XV.      TECHNOLOGY UPGRADATION
15.1     The technological upgradation of the SSI units in India has been quite slow. There are a number of factors that
are responsible for this. The Indian market has so far been basically a sellers' market. Therefore, entrepreneurs have not
made any efforts for modernisation. Moreover, there is non-availability of proper information regarding latest
technologies and their suppliers. There is inadequate availability of credit for investment in technological upgradation
and testing facilities are also not readily available. Even the technological institutions set up for assisting the small scale
industries themselves lack sophistication and coordination amongst each other.
(a) For effective technological upgradation in Indian SSI units, the Committee recommends that the partnership
approach to develop linkages between large and small enterprises be strengthened.
(b) Technology Bureau for International Industrial Partnerships and Technology Bureau for Small Enterprises,
Delhi has been providing useful services for technology upgradation in the small scale units. These organisations
need to be strengthened further and their activities need to be marketed / advertised in an effective manner. The
small scale industries in India have added strength to the industrial infrastructure and have been the engine of
growth for industrialisation. However, they are known for producing poor quality products. This makes the Indian
goods less competitive in the international markets.
(C)  The Committee observes that Government has set up a number of organizations for the purpose of
technological upgradation and quality improvement in the SS1 units. However, most of these facilities are either
non-functional or grossly under-utilised. There is an urgent need to revamp the whole system and make it effective
and beneficial to the small industries.
(d)               The Committee further recommends that quality training to significantly improve quality by creating
awareness among personnel about meeting customer requirements, standardizing processes, training operatives and
enforcing technical discipline should be institutionalized. There is a need to conduct a comprehensive research
study in a sample of SSI units to determine areas of waste and non-value adding activities and develop
methodology for quality improvement and cost reduction programmes. Further 1SO 9000 certification. may be
made more attractive to introduce quality-consciousness among small entrepreneurs. BIS standards may also be
upgraded from time to time in tune with the developments in quality worldwide.

16.2     The Committee therefore, recommends that instead of a plethora of labour laws, a single unified Act with simple

be kept outside the purview of the labour law. Instead of the complex Industrial Disputes Act, a simpler law to govern
the relationship between the Employer and the Employee be made applicable. The Shops and Establishments may also
be suitably modified.

XVIII. DE-RESERVATION OF SSI ITEMS
18.1     As required by WTO, India   removed all quantitative restrictions (QRs) by 31st March 2001.The Union Minister
for Commerce announced the removal of restrictions while announcing the EXIM policy for 2002-07. While the impact
of the removal of QRs is being felt directly by industries, which were earlier protected, there is likely to be greater
impact on the SSls, especially with regard to their competitive ability and integration with the global markets against the
opportunities of an expanding global market.
18.2     The policy of reservation, was not brought as a measure of protection alone, but was brought for some other
factors as well such as provisions of employment opportunities, development of industrial activities in the backward and
rural areas, utilization of local raw-materials, restraining migration of labour etc. Large industries and MNCs are not
barred from manufacturing the reserved items.  They have only to adhere to the stipulation that 50% of their production
of the reserved items should be exported, which they could easily do with their latest technologies and their professional
management. 
18.3    De-reservation of over 50 items which were marked for exclusive production in the SSI sector has hit hard such
affected and related units.  The Committee   fails to see any supportive and promotional measure in the latest Budget for
such affected units.  It is to be noted that the Government had accepted the Abid Hussain Committee Report in full in
1997.  The Abid Hussain Committee recommended that the abolition of reservation should accompany a support
package for the small industries, which include equity support, interest rate concessions, technology assistance etc.  The
Abid Hussain Committee, therefore, recommended allocation of Rs. 500 crore per year i.e. Rs.2, 500 crore over the next
five years for the purpose.
18.4     The Committee feels that the Government should have given such a package to the affected units. This may
include timely and low cost credit; export assistance and proper infrastructure facilities. After giving the package, a time
frame may be simultaneously given to such affected units to enable them to fight for survival.  In the absence of such
package, the Committee feels the units might be hard-pressed to survive.  Moreover, effecting dereservation without any
package will bring deleterious socio economic changes as reservation directly affects employment and economic
growth.

            The Committee further recommends that compulsory printing of manufacturing date, maximum retail price (in
Indian rupees) and composition of the products, by foreign exporters should be introduced. This would, of course, be
compatible with the national obligation under WTO, as domestic manufacturers are already required to comply with
these requirements.
(Para 11.8)
              The Committee recommends that all banks should take effective steps to help sick SSIs restructure themselves. 
The Committee observes that the abolition of Sick Industries Companies Act (SICA) so as to facilitate prompt winding
up of unviable enterprise and swift redeployment of their resources in production remains a promise. Similarly, on the
Competition Law, nothing has been done. It has reached only the stage of Parliamentary consideration. It has not
become a law. 
(Para 12.4)
              The Committee recommends that action may be taken in regard to Abolition of Sick Industries Companies
Act.  Further, Ministry should endeavour to see that Competition Law is enacted soon.
In order to revive sick industries, the Committee recommends further: -
(a)
             A special fund may be created for rehabilitation of sick SSls and the commercial banks may earmark a
portion of loans to ailing SSls.
(b)            The State Level Inter Institutional Committees (SLIICs) need to be revitalised and DICs may be used as
a forum to redress the grievances regarding delays in rehabilitation.
(c)             An Arbitration Clause may also be included in all borrower-lender arrangements in terms of Indian
Arbitration Act to avoid protracted litigation and costs. Although Entrepreneurship Development through
small enterprises is basically owner-managed, a significant number of them do employ persons for
performing managerial functions. The SSI units on the growth path should encourage their key personnel
to think and work more as entrepreneurs than as mere employees.
(Para 12.5)
In view of the above, the Committee feels that there is need for ensuring harmonisation of tax structure by
providing the following: -
(a) Rationalisation of duty may be ensured on finished goods vis-a-vis their raw materials or intermediate
goods.          
(b)
   Capital Gains Exemption may be given to sick SSI units selling off their fixed assets to repay bank loans.
(c) The coverage of Excise Duty Exemption Scheme may be made available to all the items produced by the small-
scale units.
(d)  Under MRP based assessment an additional 10% rebate may be allowed to SSI units. Rationalisation of customs
duty on raw materials/intermediate goods and finished goods for Uninterrupted Power Supplies (UPS),
components/parts of domestic electrical appliances, components/parts of auto bulbs, umbrella components,
plastic raw materials, lead ingots, electric copper wires, parts and components of RF and IF coils and reduction

of custom duty on low carbon Ferro chrome and linear alkyl benzene (LAB) may also be done.   
 (Para 13.3)
The Committee recommends that banks and other financial institutions provide marketing oriented financial
assistance to small scale sector, particularly for advertising, product promotion and setting up of regional marketing
offices. Factoring services by the banks may also be given greater priority.
(Para 14.3)
           The Committee further recommends that: -
(a)    Establishment of a Marketing Development Fund with a minimum corpus of Rs 500 crore should be made.
(b)   Engagement of marketing experts by State Financial Corporations and banks for appraisal of projects may be
done.
(c)    Consultancy by banks to small scale units regarding formulation of their marketing plans may be taken up.
(d)   Organisation of exhibition events for SSI products in major cities of the country and abroad may be done.
(e)    Appointment of a central level educational institution for designing of short-term courses on specific aspects of
marketing and other management aspects may be made.
(f)     A well planned strategy at the national level for developing exports from small scale industries sector, including
identification of sub-sectors with high export potential may be carried out.
(g)    Recognition of marketing companies as small scale enterprises and provision of institutional credit facilities to
them for the necessary infrastructure and purchase of goods may be done.
(Para 14.4)
(a)        For effective technological upgradation in Indian SSI units, the Committee recommends that the partnership
approach to develop linkages between large and small enterprises be strengthened.
(b) Technology Bureau for International Industrial Partnerships and Technology Bureau for Small Enterprises, Delhi
have been providing useful services for technology upgradation in the small scale units. These organisations need to be
strengthened further and their activities need to be marketed / advertised in an effective manner. The small scale
industries in India have added strength to the industrial infrastructure and have been the engine of growth for
industrialisation. However, they are known for producing poor quality products. This makes the Indian goods less
competitive in the international markets.
(c)        The Committee observes that Government has set up a number of organizations for the purpose of technological
upgradation and quality improvement in the SS1 units. However, most of these facilities are either non-functional or
grossly under-utilised. There is an urgent need to revamp the whole system and make it effective and beneficial to the
small industries.
(d)        The Committee further recommends that quality training to significantly improve quality by creating awareness
among personnel about meeting customer requirements, standardizing processes, training operatives and enforcing
technical discipline should be institutionalized. There is a need to conduct a comprehensive research study in a sample
of SSI units to determine areas of waste and non-value adding activities and develop methodology for quality
improvement and cost reduction programmes. Further 1SO 9000 certification. may be made more attractive to introduce
quality-consciousness among small entrepreneurs. BIS standards may also be upgraded from time to time in tune with
the developments in quality worldwide.
(Para 15.1)
 
            The Committee observes that the present structure of labour laws does not encourage efficient performance by
the SSls. Managements find it difficult to manage their human resources optimally because of the constrained labour
laws. As of now, the same set of labour laws is applicable to all industrial undertakings, irrespective of their size.
(Para 16.1)

            The Committee, therefore, recommends that instead of a plethora of labour laws, a single unified Act with
simple provisions understandable by the entrepreneurs of SSI units be legislated. SSI units employing upto 50 persons
should be kept outside the purview of the labour law. Instead of the complex Industrial Disputes Act, a simpler law to
govern the relationship between the Employer and the Employee be made applicable. The Shops and Establishments
may also be suitably modified.
(Para 16.2)
            The Committee further observes that the existing social security legislations such as Employees' Provident Fund
& Miscellaneous Provisions Act, Employees State Insurance act, Maternity Benefits Act, Workmen's Compensation
Act, and the Payment of Gratuity Act are very cumbersome for entrepreneurs of small scale units to understand and
comply with. The Committee therefore recommends that instead of so many social security legislations, a
comprehensive Social Security Scheme be formulated for providing for one insurance cover to each workman. The
small scale units should be able to devote more time to quality management rather than inspector management.
(Para 16.3)
 
            The Committee observes that at present, there are several Government agencies to deal with small scale
industries in India. These include Ministry of SSI & ARI, Office of Development Commissioner (SSI), Small Industries
Development Organisation, Small Industries Service Institutes, National Small Industries Corporation, Small Industries
development Bank of India, Product-cum-process Development Centres, Regional Testing Centres, District Industries
Centres, State Financial Corporations, State Industrial Development Corporations, State Small Industries Development
Corporations, etc.
(Para 17.1)
 
            The Committee, therefore, recommends that roles of all these organisations be re-evaluated and clearly defined.
It needs to be ensured that their activities do not overlap each other. There should also be co-ordination in the activities
of these agencies. Most importantly, all of these should be able to provide effective service to the small scale sector.
 (Para 17.2)
 
            The Committee feels that the Government should have given such a package to the affected units. This may
include timely and low cost credit, export assistance and proper infrastructure facilities. After giving the package, a time
frame may be simultaneously given to such affected units to enable them to fight for survival.  In the absence of such
package, the Committee feels the units might be hard-pressed to survive.  Moreover, effecting dereservation without any
package will bring deleterious socio economic changes as reservation directly affects employment and economic
growth.
(Para 18.4)
 
            The Committee recommends that unless state governments play a proactive role in creating infrastructure for
industries, integration and harmonization of villages with industrial development can not be achieved. Active
participation of state governments, NGOs and SSI Associations should be ensured by providing appropriate
encouragement to them. This is in keeping with the Industrial policy announced in 1991to give special thrust to the
promotion and strengthening of small tiny and village industries.
(Para 19.3)
           The Committee, therefore, recommends that stringent action should be taken against the erring large companies
which have failed to make payment to SSIs in due time.   Necessary amendment for taking punitive   action may also
be   contemplated in the Delayed Payment Act.
(Para 20.3)

banks   and should prescribe that no loan asset would become NPA even if the loan installments or interest remains

            The Committee therefore, recommends that in order to protect small scale sector from multinational companies
and others, a certain % of items, say 33% should be purchased by Central and State Government Departments/agencies
specially when the items reserved for SSI sector have been withdrawn and majority of the items have been put on OGL
